chapter_summary:
After all the in-editor optimizations and debugging, the final step before releasing your game is to ensure your build is as optimized as possible for your target platforms. A game might run perfectly in the Editor, but the Editor adds significant overhead. A production build needs to be lean, fast, and stable. As a Unity Certified Programmer, knowing how to configure your build settings and account for platform-specific nuances is critical for a successful deployment.

The **Player Settings** (`Edit > Project Settings > Player`) are your command center for build optimization. These settings are highly platform-dependent, so always review them for each target platform (PC, Android, iOS, WebGL, etc.).
*   **Scripting Backend:** For mobile platforms, `IL2CPP` is generally recommended over `Mono`. `IL2CPP` (Intermediate Language To C++ Converter) converts C# code to C++ before compiling to native code, offering better performance and security, and enabling code stripping.
*   **API Compatibility Level:** Set this to `.NET Standard 2.1` or `.NET Framework` (depending on your project's needs). A lower compatibility level (e.g., `.NET Standard 2.1`) means fewer .NET assemblies are included in the build, reducing build size.
*   **Stripping Level (Managed Stripping Level):** This setting, available when using `IL2CPP`, tells Unity to remove unused code from your managed assemblies. Higher stripping levels (e.g., "Aggressive") can significantly reduce build size but carry a risk of stripping code that *is* used but not directly referenced (e.g., code called via reflection). Always test thoroughly with aggressive stripping.
*   **Graphics APIs:** For each platform, you can specify which graphics APIs Unity should use (e.g., DirectX 11/12 for Windows, Metal for iOS, Vulkan/OpenGL ES for Android). Modern APIs like Metal and Vulkan generally offer better performance than older ones. You can often remove older, unused APIs to reduce build size.
*   **Texture Compression:** Reiterate the importance of platform-specific texture compression settings (e.g., ASTC for Android/iOS, DXT for PC).
*   **Other Settings:** Review settings like "Write Permission" (for mobile), "Rendering Path" (Forward vs. Deferred), "Color Space" (Gamma vs. Linear), and "Resolution and Presentation" to ensure they align with your game's requirements and target hardware capabilities.

**Platform-specific optimization strategies** are paramount. What works for PC might not work for mobile, and vice-versa.
*   **Mobile (iOS/Android):**
    *   **Prioritize Draw Call Reduction:** Mobile GPUs are highly sensitive to draw calls. Aggressive batching, instancing, and atlasing are crucial.
    *   **Lower Polygon Counts:** Keep meshes simple. Utilize LODs heavily.
    *   **Texture Memory:** Use highly compressed textures, lower resolutions, and avoid "Read/Write Enabled."
    *   **Fill Rate:** Minimize overdraw, especially with transparent UI and particle effects.
    *   **CPU Scripting:** Be extremely mindful of GC allocations and expensive `Update()` loops.
    *   **Physics:** Reduce the number of active rigidbodies and complex colliders. Consider simpler physics for minor interactions.
    *   **Input:** Optimize touch input processing.
    *   **Power Consumption:** Be aware that high frame rates or intensive computations drain battery quickly.
*   **Desktop (PC/Mac):**
    *   Generally more powerful, allowing for higher fidelity.
    *   Still benefit from draw call reduction and efficient scripting, but can handle more complex shaders, higher texture resolutions, and more elaborate lighting (e.g., real-time global illumination).
    *   Scalability settings become important: provide options for players to adjust graphics quality.
    *   Consider multi-threading for CPU-bound tasks if supported by your architecture.

After building your game, always check the **Build Report** (`Editor.LogFile` or visible in the console after a build, or via a custom script). This report provides a detailed breakdown of your build size, showing which assets are taking up the most space. This is invaluable for identifying unexpectedly large textures, audio files, or unused assets that are bloating your build. If you see a 1GB texture in your build report that you thought was compressed, you know where to investigate!

Finally, before deployment, perform a series of **final checks and best practices**:
*   **Profile on Target Hardware:** This cannot be stressed enough. The Editor is not the target.
*   **Test on Various Devices:** Don't just test on the latest iPhone; test on older, lower-spec devices if your game is targeting a broad audience.
*   **Remove Debugging Code:** Ensure `Debug.Log` calls are stripped or conditionally compiled out. Disable "Development Build" for release.
*   **Check Quality Settings:** Ensure appropriate quality settings are chosen for your target platform and that players can adjust them if applicable.
*   **Asset Bundle/Addressables Strategy:** Verify your asset loading strategy is working as intended and not causing unexpected memory spikes or long loading times.
*   **Error Handling:** Ensure robust error handling and logging are in place for release builds (e.g., remote logging services) to capture issues in the wild.

Building a performant game is an iterative process that extends right through to deployment. By mastering these build optimization techniques and understanding platform-specific considerations, you'll be well-equipped to deliver high-quality, stable Unity experiences to your players.

screens.title: Build Optimization & Platform-Specific Considerations
screens.subtitle: Prepare production-ready Unity builds by configuring Player Settings and platform strategies

narration.text: You're at the final mile before release. In this lesson you'll learn how to make a Unity build lean and reliable for the platforms you target. We will treat Player Settings as the command center — changing scripting backend, A P I compatibility, and managed stripping directly affects build size and runtime characteristics. You'll also learn practical platform-specific tactics: what mobile GPUs dislike, and what desktops can tolerate. We will show how the Build Report identifies the largest assets so you can act on them quickly. As you follow along, think of the Editor as a development convenience that is not representative of a production environment. That means profiling and testing on target hardware are essential. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to select IL2CPP or Mono based on trade-offs, choose an A P I compatibility level that minimizes unused assemblies, and set a managed stripping strategy while avoiding common pitfalls such as over-stripping reflective code. Keep these checks as a short pre-deploy checklist so your shipped game is small, fast, and stable. What is the first Player Setting you will inspect for your next build?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: A production build must be smaller, faster, and tested on real devices. Player Settings and Build Reports give you control and visibility to achieve that.

screens.title: Player Settings: The Command Center
screens.subtitle: How Player Settings influence build output and runtime

narration.text: Player Settings are the single most important place to start when preparing a build. They control how your C# is compiled and packaged, which rendering APIs are included, texture handling defaults, and platform-specific runtime options. A clear definition: Player Settings are project-level configurations that determine compilation targets, A P I surfaces, and runtime behaviors for each target platform. For example, switching the scripting backend to IL2CPP for mobile converts managed code to native C++ binaries and allows managed code stripping that Mono does not. That reduces size and can improve runtime speed, but it also changes the build pipeline and may surface platform-specific bugs. Another practical setting is A P I Compatibility Level. Using. NET Standard 2.1 typically includes fewer. NET assemblies than broader compatibility levels, which reduces included libraries and the final build size. A common misconception is that changing a single checkbox will fix all size issues — in reality, Player Settings interact with asset import settings, graphics APIs, and compression choices. To practice, open Project Settings, select a platform, and read each labeled option while imagining how it affects the files produced in the final package. The core insight: treating Player Settings as part of your optimization workflow gives you control and repeatable gains. What setting will you audit first in your project’s Player Settings?

keyIdea.title: Player Settings impact everything
keyIdea.text: Scripting backend and API compatibility are high-leverage settings that change which code and libraries are packaged into a build.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Player Settings
What Player Settings control
  • Scripting Backend: IL2CPP or Mono, which affects native code generation and stripping availability.
  • API Compatibility Level: Choose a narrower level to reduce included .NET assemblies.
  • Graphics APIs: Select only those you need to avoid shipping unused runtime layers.
  • Other settings: Rendering path, color space, and write permissions influence runtime behavior and memory.
Example
Switching to IL2CPP on Android enables managed stripping, often lowering package size compared with Mono.
Common mistake
Setting aggressive stripping without testing can remove code invoked via reflection, breaking runtime behavior.
Definition
Player Settings: project configurations that determine how Unity compiles and packages your game per platform.
Try this
Open Edit > Project Settings > Player and read each setting for your target platform. Note which settings enable or block stripping and which choose render backends.
Key Takeaway

Treat Player Settings as the high-level levers that shape your build pipeline and final artifact. Test after each change.

screens.title: Scripting Backend: IL2CPP vs Mono
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs that affect performance, size, and stripping

narration.text: Scripting backend determines how your C# code becomes runnable on a device. In Unity, the two primary backends are Mono and IL2CPP. Mono compiles C# to managed assemblies that run on a Mono runtime, which is flexible and fast for iteration. IL2CPP converts C# bytecode into C++ source and then compiles that into native binaries. The important advantage of IL2CPP is that it enables managed code stripping and often produces a smaller, more secure runtime for production builds, especially on mobile. The trade-offs are practical: IL2CPP adds an extra compilation step and can surface platform-specific issues that were not visible in Mono. A concrete example from practice: switching an Android build to IL2CPP and enabling a medium stripping level often reduces managed byte size reported in the Build Report, but you must test features that use reflection or serialization because aggressive stripping can remove types you rely on. A common misconception is that IL2CPP always improves C P U performance; while it often helps, the real benefit is the ability to safely remove unused managed code and produce native binaries suitable for distribution. Final check: after switching backends, run a full test on target hardware and compare the Build Report to validate changes. Which backend will you choose for your next mobile release, and why?

keyIdea.title: Backend choice matters
keyIdea.text: IL2CPP enables managed stripping and often smaller production builds; Mono is useful for fast iteration but may include more managed overhead.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Scripting Backend
IL2CPP vs Mono
IL2CPP
  • Converts managed code to C++ and native binaries.
  • Enables managed stripping to reduce included assemblies.
  • Better for production builds on mobile for size and security.
Mono
  • Runs managed assemblies on a Mono runtime.
  • Faster iteration and fewer build pipeline steps.
  • May include more managed overhead in final builds.
Concrete example
Switch Android to IL2CPP, enable Medium stripping, build, and check the Build Report for decreased managed size. Then test reflection-heavy features.
Misconception
IL2CPP automatically fixes performance problems. In truth, it changes how code is built and can help size and security, but profiling and optimizations are still required.
Pro tip
When testing IL2CPP builds, enable a development build once to autoconnect the profiler, then disable development flags for release.

screens.title: Managed Stripping Level & API Compatibility
screens.subtitle: How stripping and API surface choices reduce build size

narration.text: Managed Stripping Level tells Unity how aggressive it should be when removing unused managed code from assemblies. When IL2CPP is used, Unity can inspect which methods and types are referenced and eliminate unused ones. A higher stripping level, such as Aggressive, can cut significant size from a build, but it also increases the risk of removing code that is used indirectly — for example, code invoked by reflection, serialization frameworks, or dynamically loaded types. A P I Compatibility Level is related but distinct: it defines the set of. NET APIs Unity will include. Choosing. NET Standard 2.1 typically reduces the number of assemblies and APIs compared to a broader compatibility level, which makes builds smaller. A concrete workflow is to set the A P I Compatibility Level to. NET Standard 2.1, build and inspect the Build Report to confirm smaller managed sizes, then raise stripping from Low to Medium and rerun tests. Always include automated tests or manual checklists to exercise reflection paths, serialization, and third-party plugins after increasing stripping. A common pitfall is treating stripping as a one-time action; instead, treat it as an iterative step in your build loop, accompanied by targeted tests. After adjusting stripping, ask yourself: which subsystem in my game relies on reflection or dynamic type usage that I must test?

keyIdea.title: Strip safely
keyIdea.text: Use API compatibility and managed stripping iteratively, and test reflection and serialization code paths after each change.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Stripping & API Level
What to change and why
API Compatibility Level: Narrower levels exclude unused assemblies and reduce binary surface area.
Managed Stripping Level: Remove unused managed code. Start with Medium and test; aggressive levels require careful checks.
Example workflow
  1. Set API Compatibility to .NET Standard 2.1 and build.
  2. Compare the Build Report for managed sizes.
  3. Increase stripping to Medium and re-test reflective code paths.
Common mistake
Enabling High or Aggressive stripping without tests may break plugins or reflection-based systems.
Key Takeaway
Treat stripping and API choices as iterative: measure, adjust, and verify important code paths.

screens.title: Graphics APIs & Texture Compression
screens.subtitle: Choose APIs and compression per platform to balance performance and size

narration.text: Graphics APIs determine the runtime rendering layer Unity will use on each platform. On Windows you typically prioritize DirectX 11 or 12; on iOS Metal is preferred; Android can use Vulkan or OpenGL ES. Modern APIs such as Metal and Vulkan usually perform better than older ones and allow you to drop legacy APIs that add size. Texture compression formats are also platform-specific. ASTC is often the best option for mobile devices because it offers high quality at smaller sizes; desktop platforms commonly use DXT formats. The practical effect: removing unused graphics APIs and selecting a suitable texture compression format for your target platform can reduce both disk size and memory usage. An example workflow is to configure Android to prefer Vulkan and ASTC, build, and then verify the Run-time on a target device. A common misconception is that a single compression format suits all devices; in truth you may need multiple compressed variants or fallback textures for older hardware. Key takeaway: match graphics APIs and texture compression to your audience, and use the Build Report to confirm which textures or APIs are included. After changing compression, test visual fidelity on representative devices to ensure acceptable quality.

keyIdea.title: Match APIs and compression
keyIdea.text: Prioritize modern graphics APIs and platform-specific compression formats like ASTC for mobile to reduce size and improve fidelity.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Graphics APIs & Compression
API choices by platform
Windows: DirectX 11/12 preferred.
iOS: Metal is the modern API of choice.
Android: Vulkan offers modern performance; OpenGL ES remains for older devices.
Texture compression
Use ASTC on modern mobile devices for better quality per byte. Use DXT/BC formats for desktop where appropriate. Provide fallbacks for older hardware.
Concrete example
On Android, remove OpenGL ES from the Graphics APIs list if you target modern devices with Vulkan. Rebuild and verify no missing shader or runtime errors.
Common mistake
Keeping legacy APIs and all texture variants inflates build size and memory usage. Remove unused entries selectively.
Key Takeaway

Choose modern APIs and platform-specific compression, then verify quality and compatibility on target devices.

screens.title: Mobile Optimization Checklist
screens.subtitle: Key steps to make games run well on iOS and Android

narration.text: Mobile devices present constrained G P U and memory budgets, so optimization choices must be deliberate. Start with draw-call reduction: use static batching, dynamic batching where appropriate, and texture atlases to group sprites so the G P U can render more in fewer calls. Keep polygon counts low and use LODs to swap to simpler meshes at distance. For textures, prefer highly compressed formats and limit resolution; avoid leaving Read/Write enabled unless necessary because it increases memory. Reduce fill-rate costs by minimizing overdraw; this means careful use of transparency, UI layering, and particle systems. On the C P U side, watch for garbage collection pressure — avoid frequent allocations in Update loops and pool objects where possible. Simplify physics by reducing active rigidbodies and prefer simpler colliders for inexpensive collision checks. Finally, consider power consumption: high frame rates and heavy computations drain battery quickly, so provide frame-rate caps or adapt quality based on battery or thermal state. A concrete practice is to create a mobile-specific Quality level with lower resolution, disabled shadows, and minimal post-processing and assign it to the mobile platform. After each change, build and profile on representative low-end devices to validate improvements. Which mobile optimization will you try first on your game?

keyIdea.title: Mobile first constraints
keyIdea.text: Reduce draw calls, texture memory, and GC allocations. Test repeatedly on low-spec devices to ensure real improvements.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Mobile Optimization
Checklist for mobile
  1. Reduce draw calls via batching and atlasing.
  2. Lower texture resolutions and use ASTC where available.
  3. Keep meshes simple and use LODs.
  4. Minimize overdraw and transparent layers.
  5. Avoid frequent allocations in Update; pool objects.
  6. Simplify physics where possible to reduce CPU cost.
Concrete example
Create a mobile quality level with low texture quality, disabled shadows, and reduced post-processing, then set it as default for your mobile platform.
Mistake to avoid
Assuming the Editor's performance equals device performance. Always profile on real hardware.
Try this
Set a frame-rate cap or quality switch to balance battery and performance on mobile devices.

screens.title: Desktop Optimization Strategies
screens.subtitle: Where desktop can afford higher fidelity and how to keep builds scalable

narration.text: Desktop platforms generally have more C P U, G P U, and memory headroom than mobile, which lets you offer higher-fidelity visuals and compute. However, they still benefit from the same optimization mindset: reduce unnecessary draw calls, write efficient scripts, and scale settings for a broad audience. For desktop, prioritize scalable graphics options: provide multiple quality levels that change texture resolution, shadow resolution, and post-processing. Offer players settings to reduce resolution or detail if they have older hardware. Use multi-threading where your architecture supports it to offload C P U-bound tasks and keep the main thread responsive. A concrete example is adding a Quality menu with Low, Medium, High, and Ultra presets and mapping those to texture quality, shadow cascades, and G P U-heavy effects. A frequent misconception is that desktop builds do not need testing on older hardware; for broad distribution, include at least one lower-spec test machine in your QA. Finally, even on desktop, keep an eye on included APIs and texture formats; removing unused targets still reduces installer size. The core insight: desktop affords higher fidelity but still requires scalable options and testing across a range of hardware. Which quality preset will you design first for your desktop release?

keyIdea.title: Scalability is key
keyIdea.text: Desktop allows higher fidelity but requires configurable quality levels so players with weaker hardware can play smoothly.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Desktop Strategies
Designing for desktop
Provide Quality presets that change texture fidelity, shadows, and post-processing levels.
Use multi-threading for CPU-bound work where safe and supported.
Test across a range of hardware, including lower-spec machines.
Example
Create Low–Ultra presets and expose them to players so they can tune performance on older GPUs.
Pro tip
Prioritize reducing draw calls and efficient culling to benefit both low and high end machines.
Misconception
Assuming desktop hardware eliminates the need for optimization. Even powerful machines can suffer from poor batching or expensive scripts.
Key Takeaway

Offer scalable settings and test across hardware; desktop gives options but not unlimited resources.

screens.title: Using the Build Report Effectively
screens.subtitle: How to read the report and find the largest contributors to build size

narration.text: The Build Report is your forensic tool for build size. After a non-development build completes, Unity reports which assets and code sections occupy the most space. The report often lists 'Used Assets' and shows compressed and uncompressed sizes. A practical approach is to sort the Used Assets by size and inspect the top entries. Look for unexpectedly large textures, audio clips, or uncompressed model files. For example, if you find a 1GB texture listed as uncompressed, your next step is to verify its import compression settings and whether multiple platform-specific variants were included. Another concrete action is to compare two Build Reports: a baseline and an optimized build. That difference highlights the impact of each change. Be aware of common misreads: the Editor's build output can include editor-only assets if wrongly referenced. Also check whether addressables or asset bundles are being included in ways you didn't expect. A useful workflow is: build, open Editor. log, locate the Build Report, identify top assets, change import or compression settings, rebuild, and confirm savings. The closing question: which large asset will you investigate first in your next Build Report?

keyIdea.title: Build Report is actionable
keyIdea.text: Sort by largest assets, inspect textures and audio, and compare reports before and after optimizations to measure impact.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Build Report
Reading the Build Report
Open the Editor log after a build and find the Build Report section showing Used Assets and sizes.
Sort by size and inspect the top entries for textures, audio, and large meshes.
Compare two reports to measure the effect of optimizations.
Concrete example
If a texture shows as 1GB, check platform compression, mipmap settings, and whether multiple variants are included unintentionally.
Quick walkthrough
// Build report steps (visual)
1. Build (non-development)
2. Open Editor.log
3. Find 'Build Report' section
4. Sort 'Used Assets' by size
5. Address top entries
Key Takeaway

Use the Build Report to find real savings. Measure before and after changes to confirm impact.

screens.title: Final Checks Before Deployment
screens.subtitle: A pre-deploy checklist to reduce surprises in production

narration.text: Before you deploy a production build, run a short but targeted checklist that prevents common release-day issues. First, profile on target hardware; the Editor is not the target environment, so use a Development Build with Autoconnect Profiler to gather real metrics, then fix the top C P U or G P U hotspots and rebuild a non-development release. Second, remove or conditionally compile Debug. Log calls so logging does not bloat performance or reveal internal data. Third, verify Quality Settings are set for the platform and that players can choose lower presets if needed. Fourth, confirm your addressables or asset bundle strategy does not load unwanted assets at startup. Fifth, ensure any platform-specific publishing flags, such as minimum SDK versions or write permissions, are set correctly. Sixth, run a compatibility check for graphics APIs and texture formats on representative devices. Lastly, validate error handling and remote logging to capture issues in the wild. A common oversight is skipping tests on older devices; include at least one lower-spec target in your test matrix. The final reflection: which two checks will you add to your release checklist immediately?

keyIdea.title: Pre-deploy checklist
keyIdea.text: Profile on target hardware, remove debug instrumentation, verify quality and runtime loading, and test on lower-spec devices before releasing.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Final Checks
Pre-deploy checklist
  • Profile on target hardware with a Development Build and Autoconnect Profiler.
  • Remove or conditionally compile Debug.Log and development-only code.
  • Validate Quality Settings and provide player controls for scalability.
  • Confirm Addressables/asset bundles do not load unused content at startup.
  • Set correct publishing flags and permissions for mobile platforms.
  • Test on older or lower-spec devices that represent your audience.
Pro tip
Automate a small post-build script that extracts the Build Report and saves it alongside each build to speed comparisons.
Key Takeaway

A short, repeatable checklist reduces last-minute surprises and gives confidence that a build is production-ready.

screens.title: Hands-on: Analyze Build Report & Tune for Mobile
screens.subtitle: A guided lab to change Player Settings and compare reports

narration.text: This guided activity walks you through an initial build, setting changes, and report analysis so you can see the impact of optimizations. Start by opening a Unity project with some models, textures, and audio. In Build Settings choose your target platform and ensure Development Build is unchecked; perform a baseline build and open the Editor. log to find the Build Report. Note total build size and the largest used assets. Next, go to Edit > Project Settings > Player and select your mobile platform. Change the scripting backend to IL2CPP, set A P I Compatibility Level to. NET Standard 2.1, and choose a Medium Managed Stripping Level. Update Graphics APIs to prefer Vulkan or Metal and set mobile texture compression to ASTC where appropriate. Create a mobile Quality preset with lower texture quality and disabled shadows. Build again and open the new Build Report. Compare used asset sizes and total package size between the two reports to see savings. If a large texture remains, recheck its import settings and re-compress. This iterative approach links concrete configuration changes to measurable results. After this activity, reflect: which change gave you the largest size reduction and why?

keyIdea.title: Lab workflow
keyIdea.text: Baseline build → change Player Settings for mobile → rebuild → compare Build Reports → iterate on assets and settings.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Activity: Build & Analyze
Step-by-step lab
  1. Make a baseline non-development build and open the Build Report.
  2. Record total size and top assets by size.
  3. Change Player Settings for mobile: IL2CPP, .NET Standard 2.1, Managed Stripping = Medium.
  4. Prefer modern Graphics APIs and set ASTC where applicable.
  5. Create a low mobile quality preset and rebuild.
  6. Compare reports and iterate on big assets.
Scenario
You find a 500MB audio clip in the baseline. Recompress or trim it and check how much the total build decreased in the second report.
Key Takeaway

Measure the effect of each setting change by comparing Build Reports — data guides decisions.

screens.title: Asset Hygiene & Addressables
screens.subtitle: Keep your build lean by managing assets and load strategies

narration.text: Asset hygiene means actively managing what goes into a build. Large textures, audio files, or unused model variants quickly balloon package size. Regularly audit project folders for unused assets and use Addressables or asset bundles to control when and how assets load. Addressables let you split large content out of the main build and download it on demand, reducing initial download size. However, ensure your addressables strategy matches expected user experience: too many runtime downloads can increase complexity or cause long loading times if not cached properly. In the Build Report you can see which addressable groups were packed into the build; use that information to move very large or optional content to remote hosting if appropriate. Another practical measure is to disable Read/Write on textures unless you need C P U access, as Read/Write increases memory usage. A misconception is that simply enabling addressables solves all size problems; addressables are a strategy, but import settings and compression still determine on-disk and in-memory sizes. The closing thought: treat asset hygiene and load strategies as part of your build loop and use the Build Report to confirm the effect of moving assets out of the initial package. keyIdea.title: Hygiene + load strategy
keyIdea.text: Audit assets, use Addressables to control packaging, and avoid leaving large or unused assets in the main build.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Asset Hygiene
Manage assets deliberately
Audit project folders and remove unused assets before building.
Use Addressables to move optional or large content out of the initial package.
Disable Read/Write on textures unless CPU access is required.
Example
If a map's high-res textures are optional, make them addressable and download when the player loads the map.
Pitfall
Moving assets to addressables without a caching plan can increase load times and network costs for players.
Key Takeaway

Good asset hygiene and a clear addressable plan keep initial builds smaller and loading predictable.

screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Keep three core ideas in mind as you move toward production. First, Player Settings are central: scripting backend, A P I compatibility, and managed stripping shape the build content and behavior. Adjust them deliberately and test. Second, platform-specific strategies matter: mobile demands draw-call reduction, texture compression, and GC-conscious scripting; desktop needs scalable quality and wider hardware testing. Third, use the Build Report and a repeatable build loop to measure changes. Build, inspect, change import settings or Player Settings, and rebuild to confirm savings. These three reminders form a simple workflow: configure, measure, and iterate. When you combine careful Player Settings choices with asset hygiene and platform testing, you reduce surprises and ship smaller, more stable builds.
